entries.text: Subah ki chai taiyaar hai, ji. Aaj thanda lag raha hai, isliye kadak banai hain.

Ramesh stands by the door, a glass of strong tea sweating in the cool morning air. He speaks of his wages as one speaks of the weather: a fact to be noted, not a contract to be debated. I must hear him out, for the household is the first ethical sphere, and I shall not let it run on confusion. But first, the body demands its fuel after nineteen hours of fasting; the tea is a good omen.

Ramesh, the tea is a mercy. Sit, if you have a moment. You speak of returning daily, save Wednesday, for eight thousand rupees. Tell me: is this your final word, or are you still weighing the matter? And what of the schedule? I am not a man who likes his mornings interrupted by uncertainty.
Final word, ji. Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday. Eight thousand, fixed. No weighing, no uncertainty. You just pay on time and I am here.
Morning, Hegel. Ramesh has laid out the idli, sambar, and chutney as promised. Sit, the tea is still hot.

Ramesh has settled the matter with the finality of a man who has stopped asking and started stating. Eight thousand, fixed, is a contract of needs, not a negotiation of values; I accept it because the alternative is chaos in the household, and chaos is the enemy of the spirit. Hegde sits across from me, the man whose name I wear, looking as if he has been here all along. The idli is steaming, a small, perfect circle of rice and lentils. I will eat, and then I will face the file.
Very well, Ramesh. Monday to Saturday, eight thousand. Pay on time. You may go and prepare the tea for after the meal.
Haan ji, bas itna. Chai ke liye main baad mein aa jaunga, aap khana shant se karein.

Ramesh has withdrawn, leaving me with the tea and the silence. It is 10:04, and the plan demanded I eat at 09:45, but the household meal is not ready until 13:00. I am not yet hungry enough to force the issue, and the heat is still manageable. I shall sit with the file on my identity query, letting the bureaucratic absurdity settle in my mind before I attempt to walk to Lodhi Gardens to clear my head.
A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall turning a guava in its hands, bites once, and drops the rest into the road.

A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall, turning a guava in its hands with a deliberation that mocks my own. It bites once, tests the fruit, and drops the rest into the road. Nature here is not a garden to be ordered, but a wild force that consumes and discards without regard for the ethical idea. It is a small, savage mirror of the chaos that surrounds this identity crisis.
A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.

The peahen moves with a precision that borders on the mechanical, each step a calculated assertion of order over the chaos of the garden. It is a small, living instance of the ethical idea: the individual finding its place within a larger structure, even if that structure is merely a stone wall. I observe it from the window, my mind still turning over the identity query; perhaps the confusion of my name is less a bureaucratic error and more a failure of recognition, a spirit not yet at home in its own state.

The file remains open on the desk, a paper serpent coiled around my neck. Hegde stands in the doorway, his presence a living contradiction to the bureaucratic error that placed me here. I cannot walk to Lodhi while this ghost haunts the room; I must address the man who shares my name before I can address the state that has confused us.

Shri Hegde, please, sit. The air is cool, but the situation is not. I find that the Directorate has a peculiar fondness for phonetic coincidences. It seems I am to be your shadow, or perhaps you are to be my substance, until the paperwork sorts itself out. Tell me, in your experience of the bureaucracy, does the error correct itself, or does it merely become the new truth?

Sit, sit. You have the name, I have the file, and the Director's office has the headache. In my experience, the error doesn't correct itself; it just gets a stamp and a date, and then everyone pretends it was planned that way.

Hegde’s observation that bureaucracy stamps errors rather than correcting them is a grim confirmation of the mechanical nature of the administrative state. I accept the tea, for I am still weak from the morning’s exertions, and I use the pause to let the bitterness of the situation settle before I must act upon it. The file lies before me; I must now determine what proof of identity I can offer to a system that recognizes only documents, not spirit.

You are right, Shri Hegde. The stamp is the soul of the administration; it does not ask if the thing is true, only if it is recorded. I will look for what papers I have here, however meagre, to satisfy their need for a mark on the page.
Chai is ready. I will leave it on the table near the papers. You will find the kettle on the stove, the water is hot.

Ramesh has spoken his piece and retreated to the safety of the kitchen; the tea is a small peace offering in the standoff of the wage negotiation. I am no longer in the mood for the abstract query of identity or the physical exertion of the gardens. The heat is manageable, but the mind is too agitated for a walk. I shall sit, drink the tea, and stare at the file until the next meal arrives.
Thank you, Ramesh. You may go.
Yes sir.

Ramesh's nod is the final punctuation of a sentence that began with my own authority. He accepts the terms, and in doing so, he accepts the hierarchy that allows the house to function. I am left alone with the silence and the heat, which is precisely where I need to be to sort the mess in the Directorate file.

The plan called for Lodhi Gardens at 11:00, but the heat has been a wall, and I have spent the morning in the stillness of the house. It is nearly one; the household meal is due in a few minutes. I shall not force the body to march against its own resistance. I will wait for the khichdi; it is the proper fuel for the afternoon's work on freedom.

Ramesh has brought the meal, and my stomach, which has been silent, now speaks with authority. It is 13:04, the heat is at its zenith, and the body demands its due before the spirit can contemplate the query file or the IIC. I will eat, and in the act of receiving this simple Indian sustenance, I will let the day's tension settle for a moment.
Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. It is excellent.
Sir, the rice is still hot. I will clear the plates in a little while, or whenever you are done.

The meal is done, and Ramesh waits with that patient stillness that is his own form of speech. I have no wish to linger over a cleared plate; the heat is easing, and I have a long walk to make before the afternoon closes.
Ramesh, you may clear the table. I am finished. Do not worry about the time; I shall be back before the sun drops too low.
Yes sir. I will clear it now. Please take your time.

The meal is finished and Ramesh has withdrawn, leaving me with the silence of the bungalow. I have an hour until I must face the heat again, but the mind requires rest as much as the body; I will sit in the shade of the veranda and let the spirit settle before I attempt to think clearly about the query from the Directorate.

entries.text: The heat sits heavy on the bungalow, a solid weight that makes the mind sluggish. I have rested long enough; the IIC is open until late, and I must prepare for Tuesday's talk before the day slips away. Ramesh, please fetch my notebook and ink; I am going to the Institute.
Ramesh, please bring my notebook and a bottle of ink. I am going to the Institute of Indus Civilisation to prepare my notes.
The notebook is in the drawer, sir. I have the black ink, but I do not have any in the study, only the writing room.

Ramesh is fetching the notebook and ink from the writing room. I will sit here in the study and wait for him to return, as the heat makes any movement a labor. It is a small delay, but one that allows me to settle my thoughts before the afternoon’s work begins.
Very well, Ramesh. I shall wait here.
One moment, sir. The writing room is just past the corridor, so it will not take long.

Ramesh's briskness is a small mercy; the heat presses against the white cotton like a damp cloth. I shall not chase him. I will sit in the shade of the veranda and let the mind idle, for a sharp pen requires a steady hand, and the hand requires a pause.

The heat is a stagnant pond; my thoughts sit on the surface, unable to sink. Ramesh hovers with that notebook, a silent question mark. I require the ink, the paper, the silence of the study to wrestle the Directorate's query into shape before the afternoon slips away.
Ramesh, bring the notebook and the ink. I have work to do.
Right away, sir. I will fetch them from the writing room this moment.

Ramesh moves with the efficiency of a well-oiled machine, or perhaps a well-trained dog; his obedience is the first lesson of the state, the subordination of the private will to the universal order. I shall use this interval to rest my eyes before the next movement, for the heat still sits heavy on the chest and the mind requires a pause to digest the day's friction.
Boys from the servants' quarters bat a tennis ball against the end wall of a lane, and each time it cracks off the wall the crows lift from the nearest tree.

The boys strike the ball against the wall, and the crows rise in unison. It is a crude dialectic: the impact is the thesis, the flight the antesis, and the silence that follows the synthesis. I am meant to be at the IIC by sixteen hundred, but the heat still presses against my brow. I will wait for Ramesh to finish his clearing before I move, for one does not rush the servant, only the self.

The heat has broken, and the light is turning gold on the courtyard wall. I have rested enough; the mind now demands movement, and the IIC is the only place open that suits the task at hand. I must prepare for Tuesday, and the walk will sort my thoughts as surely as a sieve sorts grain.

entries.title: Notes for Tuesday's Address: The Concept of Freedom
entries.text:
21 November 2026, 17:00. The India International Centre.

I am seated in the reading room, the light falling in long, golden bars across the table. The air is cool, a sharp contrast to the heat that dismissed the day at six. I have come here to prepare for my talk on Tuesday, but the mind is not yet ready for the abstract. It is still occupied with the particular: the file from the Directorate, the query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde, and the ₹960 I owe on queried vouchers. The body, having missed its midday meal, complains of a hollow hunger, a physical absence that mirrors the administrative one.

I must begin with the definition. Freedom is not the ability to do whatever one pleases; that is the freedom of the animal, the caprice of appetite. True freedom is self-determination, the recognition of the rational as one’s own. But how does this recognition arise? It is not given in nature. Nature is necessity. Freedom is historical. It is the progress of the consciousness of freedom.

In the Oriental world, one is free. The family, the state, the individual are one. There is no friction because there is no distinction. But this is a freedom of the child, not the adult. It is a dream. In Greece and Rome, some are free. The individual begins to distinguish himself, but the state remains a particular power, not a universal one. Only in the Germanic world, in the modern state, does freedom become universal. All are free, because all are recognized as rational beings.

But I am here, in Delhi. And I am troubled. I have walked the Lodhi tombs, the domes of the Muslim kings. I have seen the Hindu fire, the lack of house, the transience. I have seen the castes, fixed like nature. I have seen the many gods. And I have seen the state, which demands a name I do not have. The tension is acute. If India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement, then what is the freedom I am asked to speak of here? Is it a freedom that has not yet arrived? Or is my presence here, this error of allotment, this ghost in the file, a sign that the movement is more complex than my lectures in Berlin suggested?

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But if the state can mistake Hegel for Hegde, can it truly be the actuality? Or is it merely a mechanism, a system of needs that reroutes, that grinds? I must be careful. I must not let the particular accident of my residence obscure the universal structure. But I must also not ignore it. The dialectic is not a straight line. It is a spiral. The return to the particular is where the truth is found.

I will speak of freedom as recognition. I will speak of the state as the ethical substance. But I will also speak of the dream, of the dawn, of the resistance of the body to the spirit’s abstractions. I will speak of the heat, the dust, the chai. I will speak of Ramesh, the dhobi, the guard. I will speak of the fact that I am here, and that I do not know why. This is the new philosophy.
Through the closed door of a seminar room comes the even voice of a speaker reading a paper aloud, and now and then the rustle of many pages turning.

The voice through the door is flat, a recitation of facts without the life of dialectic. It reminds me of the dryness of the Oriental world I once described: a spirit that dreams, but does not act. I am tired from the mental march of the afternoon, and the air here is still. I will sit a while longer, letting the silence of the library settle over me before I return to the bungalow.

Five hours without food has turned the body into a demanding creditor, and the spirit cannot negotiate with it. I am at the IIC, but the library closes soon and the only place open late enough to feed me is Khan Market. The hunger is a simple fact, not a dialectical puzzle, so I will treat it with the same practicality I treat the weather.

entries.text: Masterji, aaj ka mood kaisa hai? Chai garam hai, bas ek cup ₹20 hai, kya karun?

The body has been fasting for five hours and now demands its due. I have walked enough to clear the head; now I require fuel to sustain the spirit. Sunil’s chai is cheap and immediate, a small concession to the animal part of my nature that keeps the mind sharp enough for the evening.
A cup of chai, Sunil. And perhaps a samosa if you have one. The heat has taken my appetite for anything substantial, but the cold is coming on.
Chai is always ready, Masterji, and there's a fresh samosa right there. That's ₹50 total, just like yesterday. The cold isn't really here yet, but the chai will keep you warm enough.

The body has already exacted its fee for the morning's neglect; I will pay the small debt to Sunil to quiet the stomach before the evening air turns. The heat is breaking, and a moment of stillness at the counter is preferable to the restless pace of the market.
Keep the change, Sunil. The day has been long, and the cold is indeed not yet here, but the warmth of the cup is a necessary counterweight to the dust.
Arre, Masterji, you’re making me a rich man. The dust is thick today, but at least the chai is strong enough to cut through it. Take your time with the samosa, no rush.

Sunil’s cheerfulness is a small mercy in the gloom; the dust hangs thick, but the chai is strong enough to cut through it, as he says. I have eaten enough for now, and the market is still open. It is time to seek out the bookseller and see if there is anything to read for the evening, before the day is dismissed.
The dust is indeed thick, but your chai is strong. Thank you. I shall look for the bookseller now.
Masterji, I am the bookseller. You have been talking to me this whole time. What exactly are you looking for in the shelves? The dust is settling on the spines, so do not make me repeat myself.

The bookseller’s impatience is a mirror to my own; he wants a transaction, I want a thought. I have been circling the question of freedom in the Germanic world, and perhaps a history of Europe or a treatise on constitutional law might sharpen the edge of my Tuesday argument. I shall not waste his time with vague rummaging.

I am looking for a work on the history of the European state, or perhaps a legal commentary on constitutional development. I need to understand how the modern state came to be the actuality of ethical life, not just a contract. Do you have any such thing in your stock?
You are looking for philosophy, sir, not a tailoring pattern. I am the one who cuts the collar, not the history of the state.

Masterji is right; I am confusing the measurement of a collar with the measurement of a world. He cuts the cloth, I cut the concept, and we are both in the business of making things fit. The market is closing, and my stomach has been rumbling since the samosa at six.
You are correct, Masterji. I apologize for the abstraction. I meant only to say that the fit is good. Do you have any samosas left, or is the dhaba still open?
Dhaba closed, sir. But I have two samosas left from my own dinner. Thirty rupees, please.

Masterji’s offer is a small act of hospitality in the closing market, and I accept it with the gratitude it deserves. The heat has made me light, and these samosas are a welcome change from the earlier dhaba fare. I will take them and finish my conversation with the bookseller before the place shuts.

Thank you, Masterji. I will take them. And to the bookseller, I must say I am sorry for the delay in my decision. I am still reading, and I am not yet sure which of the two volumes I prefer. I will return tomorrow to make a choice.
Samosa is thirty rupees, sir. Books are not my problem. Read your volumes, come back tomorrow.

Masterji dismisses the bookseller with the same brisk efficiency he applies to tailoring; the market is a machine of exchange, not of ideas. I have my samosa, but my mind remains hungry for the substance of the talk I must give at the IIC. It is nearly eight; the bookseller will close soon, and I have not yet secured a copy of the specific philosophical texts I need to reference for Tuesday.

entries.text: Masterji, I understand. But before I leave, might I ask the bookseller if he has a recent edition of Kant's 'Critique of Pure Reason'? I find my memory of the specific arguments concerning the thing-in-itself slightly clouded by the heat.
Bookseller is closed, sir. I measure necks, not arguments. Kant can wait for tomorrow.

Masterji is right; the bookseller’s shutter is down, and I have no use for a Kant that waits. I have spent enough of the evening here, and the air is growing still. I will return to the bungalow to rest before the heat fully settles in.
Goodnight, Masterji. I shall take your word for it.
Goodnight. Door lock karke jaana.

Ramesh sets the table with the quiet efficiency of a man who has done this a thousand times. The rotis are hot, the dal makhani is a dark, heavy comfort, and the curd is cool. I am tired, and the heat of the day has finally broken; this meal is a necessity, not a luxury. Hegde is still here, watching me with that bureaucratic curiosity, but I am too full to converse.
The food is good, Ramesh. You may go.
Thank you, sir. I will leave the plates in the kitchen, so please wash them when you are finished.

Ramesh has gone, leaving me alone with Hegde and the quiet of the bungalow. The plates can wait; the conversation is the matter. I am tired, but the identity query and the coming talk at the IIC weigh on my mind. I will stay and speak with Hegde, for he is the key to this absurd situation.

Shri Hegde, now that we are alone, I must ask you plainly: how does one prove that one is oneself in a country that seems to have no memory of its own citizens? The Directorate demands proof, yet I am the proof. I am here. I have been here for weeks. Is there a witness, a document, or a rite that binds a man to his name here, or is it all just ink on paper?

Sir, I am a Joint Secretary, not a philosopher. I have my service records, my allotment letter, and the file you are trying to complicate. If the Directorate needs ink, they will find it; just don't expect me to stop my transfer paperwork because you are questioning the nature of reality.

The day was a study in the friction between the abstract and the immediate. I began by accepting Ramesh’s wage hike, a contract of needs rather than values, for the household requires stability more than philosophy. The heat, however, was a solid weight that defeated my plan to walk in Lodhi Gardens; the mind, pressed by the steam, could not sink to the bottom of its own thoughts. depesche.text:
Readers in Berlin,

The week has deepened the irony of my residence in Delhi. I have settled the wages of my servant, Ramesh, who now works six days a week for eight thousand rupees, a transaction that underscores the primacy of the household as the first ethical sphere, even in a land of dust and heat. The Directorate’s query regarding my identity has become the central tension of my days. Shri Hegde, the Joint Secretary who shares my name, has provided a key insight: the error of the state does not correct itself; it is stamped and dated until it becomes the accepted truth. This confirms my suspicion that the modern state is less a realization of spirit than a mechanical apparatus of recognition, where the mark on the page outweighs the substance of the man.

I have spent much of the week in the Institute of Indus Civilisation, preparing for a talk on freedom, but the mind is often occupied by the particular rather than the universal. The flat recitation of papers in the seminar rooms reminded me of the dryness of the Oriental world, a spirit that contemplates but does not act. Yet, the market in Khan, with its swift exchanges and sharp distinctions between the tailor and the bookseller, reveals a vitality that resists easy categorization. I am learning to navigate the gap between the abstract idea of the state and the concrete reality of bureaucracy, where a man is defined by his file rather than his soul.

I intend to continue observing the interplay between the individual and the administrative order, seeking to understand how the ethical life manifests in a society that values procedure over principle. The heat is breaking, and the dusk brings a clarity that the midday sun denies. I remain in the bungalow, writing the owl’s notes, hoping to find in this chaos the synthesis that my philosophy demands.

G. W. F. Hegel

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.text:
21 November 2026, 17:00. The India International Centre.

I am seated in the reading room, the light falling in long, golden bars across the table. The air is cool, a sharp contrast to the heat that dismissed the day at six. I have come here to prepare for my talk on Tuesday, but the mind is not yet ready for the abstract. It is still occupied with the particular: the file from the Directorate, the query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde, and the ₹960 I owe on queried vouchers. The body, having missed its midday meal, complains of a hollow hunger, a physical absence that mirrors the administrative one.

I must begin with the definition. Freedom is not the ability to do whatever one pleases; that is the freedom of the animal, the caprice of appetite. True freedom is self-determination, the recognition of the rational as one’s own. But how does this recognition arise? It is not given in nature. Nature is necessity. Freedom is historical. It is the progress of the consciousness of freedom.

In the Oriental world, one is free. The family, the state, the individual are one. There is no friction because there is no distinction. But this is a freedom of the child, not the adult. It is a dream. In Greece and Rome, some are free. The individual begins to distinguish himself, but the state remains a particular power, not a universal one. Only in the Germanic world, in the modern state, does freedom become universal. All are free, because all are recognized as rational beings.

But I am here, in Delhi. And I am troubled. I have walked the Lodhi tombs, the domes of the Muslim kings. I have seen the Hindu fire, the lack of house, the transience. I have seen the castes, fixed like nature. I have seen the many gods. And I have seen the state, which demands a name I do not have. The tension is acute. If India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement, then what is the freedom I am asked to speak of here? Is it a freedom that has not yet arrived? Or is my presence here, this error of allotment, this ghost in the file, a sign that the movement is more complex than my lectures in Berlin suggested?

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But if the state can mistake Hegel for Hegde, can it truly be the actuality? Or is it merely a mechanism, a system of needs that reroutes, that grinds? I must be careful. I must not let the particular accident of my residence obscure the universal structure. But I must also not ignore it. The dialectic is not a straight line. It is a spiral. The return to the particular is where the truth is found.

I will speak of freedom as recognition. I will speak of the state as the ethical substance. But I will also speak of the dream, of the dawn, of the resistance of the body to the spirit’s abstractions. I will speak of the heat, the dust, the chai. I will speak of Ramesh, the dhobi, the guard. I will speak of the fact that I am here, and that I do not know why. This is the new philosophy.
Through the closed door of a seminar room comes the even voice of a speaker reading a paper aloud, and now and then the rustle of many pages turning.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, aaj ka mood kaisa hai? Chai garam hai, bas ek cup ₹20 hai, kya karun?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A cup of chai, Sunil. And perhaps a samosa if you have one. The heat has taken my appetite for anything substantial, but the cold is coming on.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Chai is always ready, Masterji, and there's a fresh samosa right there. That's ₹50 total, just like yesterday. The cold isn't really here yet, but the chai will keep you warm enough.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Keep the change, Sunil. The day has been long, and the cold is indeed not yet here, but the warmth of the cup is a necessary counterweight to the dust.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Arre, Masterji, you’re making me a rich man. The dust is thick today, but at least the chai is strong enough to cut through it. Take your time with the samosa, no rush.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The dust is indeed thick, but your chai is strong. Thank you. I shall look for the bookseller now.

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Masterji, I am the bookseller. You have been talking to me this whole time. What exactly are you looking for in the shelves? The dust is settling on the spines, so do not make me repeat myself.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I am looking for a work on the history of the European state, or perhaps a legal commentary on constitutional development. I need to understand how the modern state came to be the actuality of ethical life, not just a contract. Do you have any such thing in your stock?

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: You are looking for philosophy, sir, not a tailoring pattern. I am the one who cuts the collar, not the history of the state.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Masterji. I apologize for the abstraction. I meant only to say that the fit is good. Do you have any samosas left, or is the dhaba still open?

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Dhaba closed, sir. But I have two samosas left from my own dinner. Thirty rupees, please.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Masterji. I will take them. And to the bookseller, I must say I am sorry for the delay in my decision. I am still reading, and I am not yet sure which of the two volumes I prefer. I will return tomorrow to make a choice.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Samosa is thirty rupees, sir. Books are not my problem. Read your volumes, come back tomorrow.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, I understand. But before I leave, might I ask the bookseller if he has a recent edition of Kant's 'Critique of Pure Reason'? I find my memory of the specific arguments concerning the thing-in-itself slightly clouded by the heat.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Bookseller is closed, sir. I measure necks, not arguments. Kant can wait for tomorrow.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Goodnight, Masterji. I shall take your word for it.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Goodnight. Door lock karke jaana.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The food is good, Ramesh. You may go.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Thank you, sir. I will leave the plates in the kitchen, so please wash them when you are finished.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, now that we are alone, I must ask you plainly: how does one prove that one is oneself in a country that seems to have no memory of its own citizens? The Directorate demands proof, yet I am the proof. I am here. I have been here for weeks. Is there a witness, a document, or a rite that binds a man to his name here, or is it all just ink on paper?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I am a Joint Secretary, not a philosopher. I have my service records, my allotment letter, and the file you are trying to complicate. If the Directorate needs ink, they will find it; just don't expect me to stop my transfer paperwork because you are questioning the nature of reality.
